title: Primary Function of the System
learningObjectives: Connect the maintenance setting to the member's structural function.
student: What is the primary structural function of the temporary access member in the maintenance setting?
instructor: The member provides temporary access across the pit and transfers the technician's load into the surrounding support structures.

title: External Loading
student: What is the dominant external load acting on the access member while the technician is standing on it?
instructor: The dominant external load is the technician's weight acting vertically downward at the technician's location.

title: Supports and Restraints
learningObjectives: Describe how the member transfers load at its supports.
student: How is the access member supported by the surrounding structure?
instructor: The member contacts supporting structure at its lower and upper ends. These contacts provide reaction forces that transfer the technician load from the member into the plant structure.

title: Load Path
learningObjectives: Trace force transfer through the system.
student: Trace the load path from the technician to the surrounding structure.
instructor: Technician → access member → lower and upper supports → surrounding plant structure.

title: Effect of Member Inclination
learningObjectives: Explain why inclination creates axial and transverse loading.
student: Why can an inclined member develop a different combination of internal forces than a horizontal member under the same vertical technician load?
instructor: Because the vertical load has both a component parallel to the inclined member and a component perpendicular to it. The parallel component contributes to axial force, while the perpendicular component contributes to transverse shear and bending.

title: Relevant Mechanical Response
learningObjectives: Select the internal responses needed for the stress analysis.
student: What internal responses should be considered when evaluating the stress state in the inclined access member?
instructor: Axial force, transverse shear force, and bending moment should be considered because together they create combined normal and shear stress at a cross-section.

title: Relevant Geometric Parameters
learningObjectives: Identify geometry that influences the local stress state.
student: What general geometric characteristics of the member and technician position influence the stress state?
instructor: Important characteristics include the member inclination, the technician's position along the member, the support spacing, and the cross-sectional width, thickness, and location of the point where stress is evaluated.

title: Student-Generated Structural Idealization
learningObjectives: Develop a mechanics model from the industrial context.
student: Convert the real maintenance-access system into a simplified Mechanics of Materials model. Show the inclined member, the two supports, the technician load, the selected section, and local axes along and perpendicular to the member.
instructor: A correct idealization is a straight inclined beam supported at both ends, carrying a concentrated vertical technician load. The selected section is cut through the member and local axes are defined along and transverse to the beam.
gradingNotes: Detailed symbols, dimensions, and the smooth-contact assumption are introduced only in the instructor reference model.

title: Modeling Assumptions
learningObjectives: State assumptions that define the simplified mechanics model.
student: State the assumptions used to convert the real system into the simplified mechanics model.
instructor: Static loading; straight prismatic member; technician modeled as a concentrated load; member self-weight neglected; small deformation; linear-elastic stress relations; smooth contact at the upper support; lower support represented by two reaction components; and local contact, impact, vibration, fatigue, instability, and connection details neglected.

title: Mechanics Analysis Plan
student: Explain the calculation sequence required to determine the local stress state.
instructor: Determine the support reactions; cut the member at the selected section and solve for axial force, transverse shear, and bending moment; calculate the required cross-sectional properties; determine direct axial stress, bending stress, and transverse shear stress; superimpose the normal-stress contributions; sketch the differential stress element; and interpret the dominant contribution.

title: Boundary Conditions
learningObjectives: Interpret the instructor reference model's supports.
student: From the instructor reference diagram, identify the support idealizations and reaction directions.
instructor: The lower support B is modeled with horizontal and vertical reaction components. The upper contact at C is smooth against a vertical wall, so it provides only a horizontal reaction.

title: Unknown Constraint Loads
instructor: The unknown reactions are Bx, By, and the horizontal wall reaction C.

title: Solve for Support Reactions
learningObjectives: Determine all reactions using planar equilibrium.
student: Use equilibrium of the entire member to determine the support reactions.
instructor: Moment equilibrium about B gives |C| = {{beam_C_N}} N acting to the left. Force equilibrium gives Bx = {{beam_Bx_N}} N to the right and By = {{beam_By_N}} N upward.

title: Internal Resultants at Section a-a
learningObjectives: Resolve internal resultants in local member axes.
student: Cut the member at section a-a and determine the axial force N, transverse shear force V, and bending moment M using local axes aligned with the member.
instructor: Using the left segment and the stated local sign convention: N = {{beam_N_N}} N ({{beam_N_type}}), V = {{beam_V_N}} N, and M = {{beam_M_Nm}} N·m.

title: Section Properties
learningObjectives: Determine the section properties required for normal stress.
student: Determine the cross-sectional area and second moment of area required for the normal-stress calculation.
instructor: For the rectangular section, A = bt = (600)(50) = {{beam_area_mm2}} mm2 and I = bt3/12 = {{beam_I_mm4}} mm4.

title: Normal Stress at Point A
learningObjectives: Superimpose direct axial and bending normal stress.
student: Determine the normal stress at point A by superimposing the direct axial and bending contributions.
instructor: The direct axial stress is N/A = {{beam_sigma_axial_MPa}} MPa. At yA = 12.5 mm, the bending contribution is -MyA/I = {{beam_sigma_bending_MPa}} MPa for the stated sign convention. Therefore σA = {{beam_sigma_A_MPa}} MPa.

title: Transverse Shear Stress at Point A
learningObjectives: Calculate transverse shear stress at the selected point.
student: Determine the transverse shear stress at point A using the first moment of area and the beam-shear relation.
instructor: For yA = 12.5 mm, the first moment of area of the region above A is QA = {{beam_QA_mm3}} mm3. Using τ = VQ/(Ib), τA = {{beam_tau_A_MPa}} MPa; the magnitude is {{beam_tau_A_abs_MPa}} MPa.

title: State of Stress at Point A
learningObjectives: Represent the calculated stress state on a differential element.
student: Sketch the resulting stress state on a differential element at point A.
instructor: The beam model gives σx = {{beam_sigma_A_MPa}} MPa, τxy = {{beam_tau_A_MPa}} MPa, and σy = {{beam_sigma_y_MPa}} MPa. Complementary shear stresses must be shown with directions consistent with the selected sign convention.

title: Engineering Assessment and Recommendation
learningObjectives: Identify the dominant stress contribution and recommend a mechanics-based change.
student: Which stress contribution dominates at point A, and what mechanics-based change would most directly reduce it?
instructor: The bending contribution dominates the normal stress at A; the axial contribution is much smaller and transverse shear is small. Increasing section thickness is effective because I varies with t3 for the assigned bending orientation. Reducing the technician moment arm or changing the support geometry would also reduce the bending contribution.
